en: the practice of the parasol-like conduct; the conduct of one who holds the parasol of the Dharma.

Those who attain victory but squander their father’s earned wealth in vain obtain no fruit whatsoever. For this very reason, modern youths, devoid of such conduct and unable to acquire the traditional methods of study like the noble-minded scholars of old, become incapable even of sustaining themselves. To dispel the despondency of even a few individuals in such a wretched condition, we—students studying in this school established with a righteous endowment for students by the supremely compassionate Śrī Mūlaka Mahārāja (whose name is truly significant as he is the root of all dharma)—who were encouraged by His Highness Keralavarman Deva (adorned with various titles and possessed of great majesty), a crest-jewel among the assembly of wise men, whose poetic compositions, rich with aesthetic flavor, surpass even nectar and bring immense delight to learned men and others alike; we, being unable to do anything more than express our gratitude, offer only this prayer: [The remainder of the text follows as a formal benediction.]

He who, having been examined by the keen intellect of the illustrious Keralavarman, has taken up the foundation of righteousness through his excellent undertakings, protects the earth while making it like heaven itself; he who, through the excellence of dharma initiated by the wisdom of Bṛhaspati, [upholds the world].
May the illustrious King Mūlaka be victorious and happy as long as the moon and stars endure.

Trivendram, Trivaṅkuram; Ālavakasūttam.

Homage to that Blessed One, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Thus have I heard:

at one time the Blessed One was dwelling in Āḷavī, in the abode of the yakṣa Āḷavaka. Then the yakṣa Āḷavaka approached the place where the Blessed One was; having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
"Come out, ascetic!"
"Excellent, friend," [said the Blessed One] as he went out.
"Enter, ascetic," [said the other].
"Excellent, friend," [replied] the Blessed One as he entered.
A second time, the yakṣa Āḷavaka said this to the Blessed One:
"Go out, ascetic!
"Very well, friend," the Blessed One replied, and he went out.
"Enter, O Śramaṇa!
"Very well, friend," said the Blessed One, and he entered.
For a third time, the yakṣa Āḷavaka spoke these very same words to the Blessed One:
"Go out, ascetic!
"Very well, friend," said the Blessed One, and he went out.
"Enter, ascetic!"
"Excellent, friend," said the Blessed One, and he entered.
For a fourth time, the Yakṣa Āṃalaka addressed the Blessed One in this very same way:
"Go out, ascetic!"
"Indeed, O Bandhu, I shall not go forth; do whatever you must do. [Bandhu replied:

"O Śramaṇa, I shall ask you a question. If you do not answer me, I will either cast your mind into confusion, or I will split your heart, or else, seizing you by the feet, I will throw you to the other side of the Gaṅgā."

"Indeed, friend, I do not see anyone in this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, who could shake my mind, split my heart, or seize me by the feet and cast me to the other shore of the Gaṅgā. Nevertheless, friend, ask whatever you desire.
"What indeed is the supreme wealth for a person in this world?
What indeed is well-conducted behavior that brings about happiness?"
"What indeed is the most excellent among flavors? How do they say that life is the best kind of life?
"Faith is the wealth of a person; it is the most excellent."
Dharma well-practiced brings happiness;
truth is indeed the most excellent of flavors; they say wisdom is the best life of the living."
How does one cross the ocean? How indeed does one transcend suffering?
And how, indeed, does one become completely purified?
Through faith one crosses the flood;
through heedfulness, the ocean;
through vigor, one transcends suffering.
It is purified by wisdom.
How indeed does one obtain wisdom? How does one find wealth?
How does one attain fame? How does one bind friends?
And how, having passed from this world to the next world, does one not grieve after death?
One who has faith in the Dharma of the Arhats attains Nirvana;
being attentive and discerning, one who desires to hear gains wisdom.
One who acts appropriately, bears his burden, and rises up finds wealth;
through truth he attains fame, and by giving, he binds friends.
Thus, having passed from this world to the next, he does not grieve.
The householder who possesses these four qualities—
truth, righteousness, fortitude, and generosity— is indeed one who does not grieve after death.
(4) "Come now, ask other ascetics and brahmins separately whether there is anything further than truth, dharma, renunciation, and patience."
"How indeed shall I now question the various recluses and brahmins?
For today I have come to understand that goal which pertains to the future life. (1)
"Alas, for my sake the Buddha has come to Ālāvī for his dwelling!
Today I understand where a gift yields great fruit.
Thus, I shall wander from village to village and from town to town."
I pay homage to the Fully Awakened One and to that Dharma which is the excellent Dharma.
Thus ends the Āḷavaka-sūtra. By Vidhuśekhara Śarmā,
inhabitant of Sāharāma.
O noble ones of pleasing speech! May you remember this jewel of a verse by Bhavabhūti:
"Where there was once a riverbed, there is now the current of rivers;
the density and sparseness of the trees have undergone a complete reversal."
"Having not seen this forest for a long time, I consider it as if it were another;
yet the dwelling of these mountains makes me firm in the thought that 'this is indeed that very place. Thus.

Furthermore, with the passage of time, even mountains become like dust. Therefore, it is not surprising that Sāhāra, the crown jewel of the desert, was once a most prosperous great city, endowed with lakes, rivers, and other features, six thousand years ago. Recently, forty-five Egyptian scientists, having traversed the entire Sāhāra region, have determined this. Because it "takes away everything" (*sarvaṃ harati*), the name of this desert is etymologically appropriate as *Sāhara*. The word *tat* [in the original text] refers to a well-known subject.
